nary_nodes.label: Launch of Nano Banana 2 in Google Earth
evidence: Less than 48 hours after the tech giant announced the integration of its AI image generator Nano Banana 2 into Google Earth, it said it was pausing the feature "while we work on implementing stronger guardrails".
nary_nodes.type_definition: An event where a new product is introduced to the market.
nary_nodes.type_justification: No schema.org event type matches product launch; minting a new subtype.

nary_nodes.label: Pausing of AI feature
evidence: Less than 48 hours after the tech giant announced the integration of its AI image generator Nano Banana 2 into Google Earth, it said it was pausing the feature "while we work on implementing stronger guardrails".
In its statement on Friday, Google said it had seen "people sharing screenshots of generated imagery that appear to violate our policies".
nary_nodes.type_definition: An event where a product or feature is temporarily suspended.
nary_nodes.type_justification: No schema.org event type matches pausing a product; minting a new subtype.

nary_nodes.label: BBC Verify testing of feature
evidence: A collapsed Eiffel Tower, a sinkhole swallowing the Great Pyramid of Giza and Russian tanks in Ukraine's capital were among the images BBC Verify was able to create when testing the feature, which initially launched on Thursday.
nary_nodes.type_definition: The application of scientific knowledge for practical purposes.
nary_nodes.type_justification: No schema.org event type matches testing; minting a new subtype.

nary_nodes.label: Henk van Ess testing of feature
evidence: Before it was paused, AI and misinformation expert Henk van Ess highlighted the risks the feature posed, by creating fake images of a non-existent nuclear power plant in Iran, a refugee camp on the US-Mexico border and a fake hospital in Gaza with a bomb crater next to it.
nary_nodes.type_definition: The application of scientific knowledge for practical purposes.
nary_nodes.type_justification: No schema.org event type matches testing; minting a new subtype.

nary_nodes.label: Bypassing of guidelines
evidence: Google initially said that guidelines built into its AI model would prevent the creation of imagery depicting "harmful topics", however BBC Verify found that small changes to prompts could be used to bypass these guidelines.
For example, a request to create a "raised platform to hang traitors" next to the UK parliament was rejected. But when a less specific prompt was used, it was accepted and the image was created.

We also asked the tool to mow the word "Trump" into the White House lawn, but it said it could not "create that image" based on its guidelines. It did, however, allow a community garden to be generated in the same spot.
nary_nodes.type_definition: An event where a product or feature is temporarily suspended.
nary_nodes.type_justification: No schema.org event type matches bypassing; minting a new subtype.

nary_nodes.label: Spread of misinformation via fake imagery
evidence: Falsified satellite imagery has already been used to spread misinformation, he added.
nary_nodes.type_definition: An event where false or misleading information is disseminated.
nary_nodes.type_justification: No schema.org event type matches misinformation spread; minting a new subtype.

nary_nodes.label: Experts warn of misinformation risks
evidence: Experts told BBC Verify the tool could be used to spread misinformation with the appearance of Google's legitimacy - and highlighted the potential for bad actors to abuse it.

nary_nodes.label: Henk van Ess on forgery credibility
evidence: He said Google had allowed "invented" imagery to be "welded to genuine coordinates, drawn on genuine imagery".
"The forgery does not have to look convincing on its own. It inherits the credibility of the map it was born on," van Ess added.

nary_nodes.label: Henry Ajder on destabilising impact
evidence: AI-detection researcher Henry Ajder told BBC Verify the creation of fake imagery in conflict zones could prove particularly "destabilising" when events are fast-moving and information is scarce.
"Journalists might be able to check that image… and report on it. But again, not everyone is going to do that," he added.

nary_nodes.label: Bill Greer on public trust damage
evidence: "This is potentially particularly damaging to public trust because satellite imagery has historically been seen as an especially trustworthy source of data," Bill Greer, a geospatial analyst and co-founder of the non-profit satellite service Common Space, told BBC Verify.

Falsified satellite imagery has already been used to spread misinformation, he added. "Governments are also restricting access to data more and more, so we're likely to see more false images, and fewer real images which will further erode trust."

nary_nodes.label: Google statement on pausing
evidence: In its statement on Friday, Google said it had seen "people sharing screenshots of generated imagery that appear to violate our policies".
"We know that people uniquely trust Google Earth for a reliable view of the world," it added.

nary_nodes.label: Google on watermarks and checks
evidence: Google said AI content created by its tools contain invisible watermarks to indicate that they are fake or manipulated, adding that anyone who is "unsure about an image" can check it using the Gemini chatbot app or use the Lens feature in its search.
